group.passage: To reject someone who wants to befriend you, you may say this: “I’ve got enough friends already.” Essentially, this response implies that you cannot develop any more friendship and it is often used as a gentle way to turn down romantic advances while still leaving the door open for a friendly connection. It touches on the idea that there may lie a limit on the number of relationships, which is in keeping with the theory of Dunbar’s number. Dunbar’s number, introduced by British anthropologist Robin Dunbar, suggests that humans can effectively maintain about 150 connections at once. Convinced that there was a ratio between brain sizes and group sizes, Dunbar proposed this idea by studying non-human primates’ grooming behavior, an important social behavior of primates. From the research, Dunbar concluded that the size of the neocortex—the part of the brain connected with cognition and language—is linked to the size of a social group. He applied this principle to humans, revealing consistency in the “magic number” 150 across various human groupings. The significance of Dunbar’s number lies in its ability to predict the point at which maintaining meaningful connections becomes challenging. Beyond 150, social groups may face difficulties with cohesion and stability. While Dunbar’s number offers a valuable guideline, individual social needs and external factors must also be considered. Social media and online platforms have revolutionized our ability to connect, potentially expanding our networks beyond the traditional limit. However, the nature of these connections differs from the intimate and lasting relationships within a core social group. Another advantage of understanding Dunbar’s number lies in its implications for urbanization. Large cities often foster alienation and tension due to their fragmented nature. At this, the concept suggests creating smaller, tightly-knit communities within urban settings to enhance a stronger sense of belonging and improve overall social well-being. All in all, Dunbar’s number provides valuable insights into the dynamics of human social interactions. As we continue to develop social relationships, Dunbar’s number serves as a guiding principle for fostering meaningful connections in a rapidly changing world.
